extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (metaphysics/ethics), especially those interested in the will, freedom, and morality
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a philosophical treatise exploring the relation between the will (thing-in-itself) and phenomena: immortality, fear of death, assertion vs denial of the will, freedom vs necessity, character, motives, and repentance. The text develops conceptual distinctions (intelligible vs empirical character) and their ethical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality as thing-in-itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Every individual is transitory only as phenomenon, but as thing-in-itself is timeless, and therefore endless; death destroys the illusion which separates his consciousness from that of the rest: this is immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that 'immortality' here is not permanence in time but the timeless nature of the will as thing-in-itself. The passage contrasts temporal persistence (which does not follow) with the timeless exemption of the will; implication: consolation for egoism cannot rest on temporal permanence but on this metaphysical status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical knowledge can overcome fear of death
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical knowledge of the nature of the world ... could even at this point of view overcome the terror of death in the measure in which reflection had power over direct feeling in the given individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides how abstract, reflective comprehension (seeing the whole rather than the particular) can prevent the thought of death from poisoning life. Examples cited: Bhagavad-Gita (Krishna raising Arjuna), Goethe's Prometheus. Caveat: such knowledge may fail when death is presented concretely and feeling prevails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion vs denial of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: The assertion of the will means that ... this knowledge does not by any means check its volition; ... The denial of the will shows itself if, when that knowledge is attained, volition ends, because the particular known phenomena no longer act as motives for willing, but the whole knowledge ... becomes a quieter of the will; and thus free, the will suppresses itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes two ethical responses once knowledge of the will's nature is attained: continued willing (assertion) and suppression/self-denial (denial). The denial is described as a quietering of motives by comprehensive knowledge and is linked to phenomena like holiness and self-renunciation (to be developed later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the will (thing-in-itself) vs necessity of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The will as such is free, follows from the fact that ... it is the thing-in-itself ... The phenomena ... are subordinate to the principle of sufficient reason ... thus ... absolutely necessary. Everything is as phenomenon absolutely necessary: in itself it is will, which is perfectly free to all eternity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents the proposed solution to the freedom/necessity contradiction: freedom pertains to the will as thing-in-itself (outside the principle of sufficient reason), while necessity pertains to the world of phenomena (objects). This is a central metaphysical criterion: distinguish levels (thing-in-itself vs phenomenon) when attributing freedom or necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of sufficient reason governs phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: All that belongs to the phenomenon ... is in one aspect reason, and in another aspect consequent; and in this last capacity is determined with absolute necessity, and can, therefore, in no respect be other than it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that every event or characteristic in the phenomenal world can be shown to follow from reasons (causes, grounds); implication: human actions as phenomena are necessarily determined by motives and character, analogous to causal laws in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human person (phenomenon) is not free in actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The person is never free although he is the phenomenon of a free will; for he is already the determined phenomenon of the free volition of this will, and, because he enters the form of every object, the principle of sufficient reason, he develops indeed the unity of that will in a multiplicity of actions, but ... this multiplicity exhibits in itself the regular conformity to law of a force of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that individual actions are necessarily determined by the person's empirical character and motives. Although subjectively felt as free ('a priori'), actions are, objectively, necessary given character. Advises caution against conflating subjective feeling of freedom with metaphysical freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion of empirical freedom of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellect knows the conclusions of the will only a posteriori and empirically; therefore when a choice is presented, it has no data as to how the will is to decide ... it seems to the intellect that in a given case two opposite decisions are possible for the will. This is just the illusion of the empirical freedom of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains epistemic source of the illusion: the intellect lacks access to the intelligible character (the will's inner nature), so decisions appear undetermined relative to our knowledge. Practical implication: apparent openness of choice is subjective, not an indication of metaphysical indeterminacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligible character vs empirical character
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligible character of every man is to be regarded as an act of will outside time ... and the manifestation of this act of will developed and broken up in time and space ... is the empirical character as it exhibits itself for experience in the whole conduct and life of this man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the immutable, timeless core (intelligible character) from its temporal manifestations (empirical character). Methodological note: when explaining or predicting behavior, one must recognize the empirical character as repeated manifestations of an underlying intelligible disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions determined by character and motives (predictability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If only the empirical character and the motives were completely given, it would be possible to calculate the future conduct of a man just as we can calculate an eclipse of the sun or moon. As Nature is consistent, so is the character; every action must take place in accordance with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a criterion for prediction: sufficient knowledge of empirical character plus motives yields deterministic prediction of actions. This functions as an explanatory standard for human behavior in this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives act only through knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The motives which determine the manifestation of the character or conduct influence it through the medium of knowledge. For motives to act, it is necessary not only that they should be present, but that they should be known; ... causa finalis movet non secundum suum esse reale; sed secundum esse cognitum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that presence of motives is insufficient; the subject must know them (or believe them) for them to operate. Examples: ignorance of suffering reduces influence; belief in future reward can motivate giving from egoism. Practical implication: changing knowledge alters which motives operate, thereby changing conduct without changing the underlying will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will is original; willing is not learned (velle non discitur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Velle non discitur. ... The will is first and original; knowledge is merely added to it as an instrument belonging to the phenomenon of will. Therefore every man is what he is through his will, and his character is original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects doctrines that make will derivative of thought or learning (liberum arbitrium indifferentiæ). Implies limits of moral education: instruction can alter means and knowledge but cannot change the fundamental will; moral reformation can redirect expression of will but not its ultimate aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repentance proceeds from corrected knowledge, not change of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance never proceeds from a change of the will (which is impossible), but from a change of knowledge. ... The discovery of this through fuller knowledge is repentance. ... Repentance thus always proceeds from corrected knowledge, not from the change of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an ethical diagnostic: remorse or corrective action indicates improved understanding of the relation between one's act and one's inmost aim, not alteration of the underlying will. Distinguishes sincere repentance (amends based on corrected knowledge) from mere anguish of conscience (pain at knowledge of oneself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and instruction can change means but not ultimate ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction, improved knowledge ... may indeed teach the will that it erred in the means it employed, and can therefore bring it about that the end after which it strives once for all according to its inner nature shall be pursued on an entirely different path and in an entirely different object ... But it can never bring about that the will shall will something actually different from what it has hitherto willed; this remains unchangeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets a practical boundary for moral influence: pedagogical or rhetorical efforts can reshape behavior and choice of means by altering knowledge, but they cannot transform the underlying striving of the will. Example: same egoistic striving may pursue different objects (worldly or imagined paradises) depending on beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral assessment must account for ignorance vs knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is corrected knowledge of the relation of an act to its special intention. ... Anguish of conscience for past deeds is anything but repentance. It is pain at the knowledge of oneself in one’s inmost nature, i.e. as will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes a criterion for judging moral change: distinguish whether a subject's change in behavior stems from corrected knowledge (worthy repentance) or merely from emotional pain. Ethical evaluation should consider whether knowledge altered the motives available to the subject.
